claims.claim: Martin kills off central characters who are richly imagined, three-dimensional portraits, which most writers could not bear to lose.
claims.source: John Lanchester, 'When did you get hooked?', London Review of Books v35 n7, 11 Apr 2013
claims.quote: richly imagined, textured, three-dimensional portraits of central characters

claims.claim: Narrative momentum slows in books four and five, which become leisurely and expansive with overlapping, simultaneous storylines.
claims.source: John Lanchester, 'When did you get hooked?', London Review of Books v35 n7, 11 Apr 2013
claims.quote: the narrative momentum of the series has slowed

claims.claim: The appeal rests on the depth, texture and thoroughness of the imagined world and the range of imaginative sympathy across a large cast.
claims.source: John Lanchester, 'When did you get hooked?', London Review of Books v35 n7, 11 Apr 2013
claims.quote: depth and texture and profoundly satisfying thoroughness

claims.claim: The Bran defenestration lands harder in the book than on screen because Bran has already been established as a viewpoint character.
claims.source: John Lanchester, 'When did you get hooked?', London Review of Books v35 n7, 11 Apr 2013
claims.quote: even more of an impact, perhaps

claims.claim: Lanchester's 4,617-word essay contains no verdict on Martin's diction, sentence rhythm or dialogue; its praise is entirely structural (unpredictability, instability, the seasons as economic metaphor), and the LRB now serves the full text without a paywall.
claims.source: John Lanchester, 'When did you get hooked?', London Review of Books v35 n7, 11 Apr 2013

claims.claim: Each chapter is narrated by a different character, so the reader's view of any character is partial, biased or wrong and must be revised as the tale evolves.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: each chapter is narrated by a different character

claims.claim: The fragmented viewpoint storytelling mirrors the theme of power fragmenting societies and individuals.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: This fragmentation in the storytelling nicely mirrors Martin’s larger theme

claims.claim: Martin replaces standard English with compound coinages such as 'sellsword' for mercenary and 'holdfast' for fort.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: the compound coinages that replace standard English

claims.claim: The diction and the spellings of names are ingeniously quasi-medieval.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: ingeniously quasi-medieval diction and spellings of names

claims.claim: Period nouns (destriers, palfreys, vair, samite) give a strong sense of the concrete reality of the world and cannot be rendered on screen.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: the perfumed language—the horses called destriers and palfreys

claims.claim: The narrative alternates distinctly Anglo-Saxon milieus with exotic 'oriental' locales, bearing traces of Scott, Conan Doyle and Costain boys' adventure stories.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: the distinctly Anglo-Saxon milieus alternating with exotic “oriental” locales

claims.claim: Tyrion's speech sets 'magnificent' destriers beside 'shit', a pointed mock-medieval deflation of romance that asks the reader to see beyond glitter to gore.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: The juxtaposition of “magnificent” and “shit” is pointed

claims.claim: The three-walled description of Qarth (animals, war, sex) reads as a sly reference to the series' own layered decor.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: a sly reference to the series itself

claims.claim: The view of court power is grimly unsentimental and Tacitean, with a tart Thucydidean appreciation of political corruption breeding narrative corruption.
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue

claims.claim: Eastern cultures are rendered with Herodotean gusto (horse-worshipping Dothraki, quasi-Assyrian city-states, Venetian Braavos).
claims.source: Daniel Mendelsohn, 'The Women and the Thrones', New York Review of Books, 7 Nov 2013 issue
claims.quote: renders the Eastern cultures in particular with Herodotean gusto
